text: Welcome to Industrial Science, course 2300506.
This first session is about choosing under uncertainty: how to make a decision before you know what will happen.
We will use one company, CellCo, for the whole course.
The course has eighteen sessions in two blocks.
Block one, in January, covers decision making, Markov analysis and network models.
Block two, in March, covers linear programming and statistical quality control.
We are here, in session one, at the start of decision making.
Every module returns to the same case, a battery cell maker called CellCo, and each session adds one decision it has to make.
These slides can be used in class or on your own.
The narration button turns this voice on or off, and the pause and replay buttons appear while it is on.
The captions button shows English captions in time with the voice. With the voice off, it shows the full text of each slide.
Auto-advance moves to the next slide when the narration ends, but interactive slides wait until you move on.
Click on a slide or press the right arrow key to go forward, and press the left arrow key to go back.
Here is the plan for the next two hours.
We spend the first part on the payoff table and five decision criteria, followed by a short activity in pairs.
After a ten-minute break, we add probabilities and calculate expected value and the value of information.
Then you will measure your own attitude to risk in the second activity.
Keep today's question in mind: CellCo must add capacity before it knows the demand. Which option should it choose, and what does the answer depend on?
CellCo makes LFP battery cells for energy storage and electric vehicles.
Its board wants two more gigawatt hours of capacity per year.
Demand three years from now may be low, medium or high, and the board has to commit before it knows which.
There are four options: a new LFP line, a sodium-ion retrofit of an existing line, a tolling contract with a partner plant, or doing nothing.
Each option is scored by its net present value over ten years, in millions of yuan.
The company and its numbers are fictional, written for teaching.
Every decision problem has four elements.
Alternatives are what you can choose. States of nature are what happens that you cannot control. Payoffs are the result of each alternative in each state.
The fourth element is the criterion, the rule that turns a table of payoffs into a choice.
The first three come from the problem. The criterion is chosen by the decision maker, and as we will see, it can change the answer.
This is CellCo's payoff table.
The new LFP line gains 260 million if demand is high, but loses 120 million if demand is low.
The tolling contract never loses money, but it never gains more than 70 million.
No option is best in every state, so the table alone does not tell us what to do.
Before the next slide, write down the option you would choose and one reason.
Here are five criteria that do not need probabilities.
Maximax takes the best case of each option and picks A, with 260. Maximin takes the worst case and picks C, the only option that never loses.
Hurwicz mixes the two with an optimism weight, alpha. With alpha equal to 0.6, it picks A.
Laplace treats the three states as equally likely, averages them, and also picks A.
Minimax regret picks B. We will build its regret table in two slides.
The data did not change. Only the rule changed, and with it the choice.
Move the slider to change alpha, the board's optimism.
At alpha equal to zero, Hurwicz is the same as maximin and picks C. At alpha equal to one, it is maximax and picks A.
The colored strip shows which option wins at each alpha. C wins below about 0.39, B wins only in a narrow band up to about 0.42, and A wins above that.
So the choice can change with a small change in optimism, which is a weakness of this criterion.
Regret is the payoff you missed by not choosing the best option for the state that happened.
For each column, subtract each payoff from the best payoff in that column.
If demand is low, the best option is C with 10, so the regret of A is 10 minus negative 120, which is 130.
Then take each option's largest regret, and choose the option whose largest regret is smallest.
That is B, with a maximum regret of 110. B is never the best in any state, but it is never far from the best.
Activity one. Work in pairs for ten minutes.
A consultant proposes a fifth option, E, a three gigawatt hour mega-line, with payoffs of minus 200, 20 and 300.
Redo the regret table with E included, and answer the three questions on the slide.
Hint: only one column gets a new best payoff.
If you are studying alone, write your three answers before you move on.
With E included, the best payoff under high demand is now 300, from E.
That raises the regret in the high-demand column for every other option.
The maximum regrets become 130 for A, 150 for B, 230 for C, 300 for D and 210 for E.
So minimax regret now picks A. E is not chosen, but adding it moved the choice from B to A.
In a board meeting, this means a proposal that everyone will reject can still change the decision. Criteria that score each option on its own do not have this problem.
Let us take a ten-minute break.
When we come back, we will add probabilities from a market study: 0.3 for low demand, 0.5 for medium and 0.2 for high.
With probabilities, we can compute the expected monetary value, or EMV, of each option.
Multiply each payoff by the probability of its state and add them up.
For A, that is 0.3 times minus 120, plus 0.5 times 80, plus 0.2 times 260, which gives 56 million yuan.
B gives 48, C gives 37, and doing nothing gives zero, so EMV picks A.
EMV assumes the board is risk-neutral: a loss of 120 million weighs exactly as much as a gain of 120 million.
Expected opportunity loss, or EOL, is the expected regret.
Weight each regret by the probability of its state. For A, only the low-demand regret of 130 counts, so its EOL is 0.3 times 130, which is 39.
For every option, EMV plus EOL equals 95.
So minimizing expected regret and maximizing expected value always give the same choice.
Now suppose a perfect forecast told CellCo the demand before it decides.
It would choose C if demand is low, and A if demand is medium or high.
The expected value with perfect information is 0.3 times 10, plus 0.5 times 80, plus 0.2 times 260, which is 95 million yuan.
The expected value of perfect information, or EVPI, is 95 minus 56, which is 39 million yuan. It equals the smallest EOL.
This is an upper limit. No market study, however good, is worth more than 39 million yuan for this decision. In session two we will price a real, imperfect survey.
Use the two sliders to change the probabilities of low and high demand. The probability of medium demand is what remains.
The bars show the EMV of each option, and the readout shows the best option and the EVPI.
Try to find the probability of low demand at which A stops being the best choice.
With the probability of high demand held at 0.2, A stays the best until the probability of low demand reaches 0.38, and then B takes over.
The choice is sensitive to the chance of low demand, which is why better information has value.
Activity two. Work on your own for five minutes.
Imagine you are CellCo's chief executive. Each line is a fair coin toss for the company: you either win the first amount or lose half of it.
Decide whether you would accept each gamble, and write your answers on paper before you click.
Then enter your answers. The slide estimates your risk tolerance, R, as the largest gamble you accept.
Keep your value of R. We will use it in a few minutes.
Utility turns a risk attitude into numbers.
With exponential utility, U of x equals one minus e to the power of minus x over R, where R is the risk tolerance.
The certainty equivalent is the sure amount that has the same utility as the gamble. It is the amount you would accept instead of taking the risk.
The dashed straight line is a risk-neutral decision maker, who uses EMV. The curves bend more as R gets smaller.
With a small R, the loss of 120 million under low demand weighs more than the gain of 260 million under high demand.
Move the slider to change the risk tolerance R, in millions of yuan, on a log scale.
Each line is the certainty equivalent of one option. The vertical line marks your R, and the readout names the preferred option.
Below an R of about 180 million, the tolling contract C is preferred. Between 180 and 835 million, the sodium-ion retrofit B is preferred.
Only above 835 million does the new LFP line A come first, which is the choice that EMV made.
As R becomes very large, each certainty equivalent approaches its EMV.
Now work in pairs for fifteen minutes.
Use your own R from the four gambles, and compute the certainty equivalents of A, B and C by hand with the formula.
Then check your answers on the previous slide.
Compare with your partner. If your choices differ, find the value of R at which you would agree.
At the end, we will count how many of you chose A, B and C. If you are studying alone, use R equal to 100 and R equal to 400.
Here are reference values to check your work.
At an R of 100 million, the certainty equivalents are minus 21.2 for A, 26.6 for B and 34.8 for C, so C is preferred.
At 400 million, B is preferred, and only at 1,000 million does A come first.
So the EMV choice, A, holds only for a board that is close to risk-neutral.
Let us summarize.
Without probabilities, the criterion decides: maximin picks C, minimax regret picks B, and maximax picks A from the same table.
With probabilities, EMV picks A at 56 million yuan, and the value of perfect information caps what any forecast is worth at 39 million.
Utility makes the board's risk attitude explicit. CellCo's choice moves from A to B to C as its risk tolerance falls.
In session two, we will use a decision tree to price an imperfect market survey, and AHP to choose CellCo's storage technology.
This slide lists today's key terms in English and Chinese, for reference.
Use the English terms in your assignments and quizzes.
To finish, take three minutes for the exit ticket.
On paper, write two sentences for CellCo's board: which option you recommend, and which number from today supports it.
Hand it in at the door. Quiz one opens online this evening.
